## Abstract

This paper focuses on the noiseless complete dictionary learning problem, where the goal is to represent a set of given signals as linear combinations of a small number of atoms from a learned dictionary. There are two main challenges faced by theoretical and practical studies of dictionary learning: the lack of theoretical guarantees for practically-used heuristic algorithms and their poor scalability when dealing with huge-scale datasets. Towards addressing these issues, we propose a simple and efficient algorithm that provably recovers the ground truth when applied to the nonconvex and discrete formulation of the problem in the noiseless setting. We also extend our proposed method to mini-batch and online settings where the data is huge-scale or arrives continuously over time. At the core of our proposed method lies an efficient preconditioning technique that transforms the unknown dictionary to a near-orthonormal one, for which we prove a simple alternating minimization technique converges linearly to the ground truth under minimal conditions. Our numerical experiments on synthetic and real datasets showcase the superiority of our method compared with the existing techniques.

## 1 Introduction

The dictionary learning problem seeks to represent data as a linear combination of a small number of basis elements, known as atoms, which are learned from the data itself. The resulting collection of atoms, known as the dictionary, can then be used for a variety of signal processing tasks Mairal et al., (2007); Liu et al., (2018), often as a plug-in replacement for classical bases based on cosines, wavelets, or Gabor filters. The advantage of a learned dictionary over these classical bases is that it is tuned to the input dataset, and can therefore provide a sparser representation for each input signal that uses fewer atoms.

The problem of learning a dictionary that provides the sparsest representation is non-convex and highly difficult to solve, both in theory and in practice. In this paper, we focus on learning a complete dictionary, whose number of atoms matches the dimensionality of the data, via the following optimization problem:

$$ \min_{\bm{X},\bm{D}}\|\bm{Y}-\bm{D}\bm{X}\|_{F}^{2}+\zeta\|\bm{X}\|_{0}. $$

Here, $\bm{Y}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$ is a data matrix whose columns are observed signals, and our goal is to find a square dictionary matrix $\bm{D}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ and corresponding sparse code $\bm{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$ to approximately represent $\bm{Y}$ while minimizing its $\ell_{0}$ pseudo-norm (denoted as $\|\cdot\|_{0}$ ) which counts its number of non-zero elements.

The ability to solve CDL to optimality would allow us to strike the best-possible trade-off between the sparsity of the representation and its quality of fit (according to the preference expressed by the parameter $\zeta>0$ ). Unfortunately, the $\ell_{0}$ pseudo-norm presents a significant difficulty, as it is not only non-convex, but also discrete and combinatorial. Even rigorously verifying that a learned dictionary is first-order locally optimal could require exhaustively enumerating all $2^{np}$ possible sparsity patterns. It is therefore understandable that the most widely-used heuristics like KSVD Aharon et al., (2006) and MOD Engan et al., (1999) do not actually guarantee convergence to an optimal solution, not even when provided with a near-optimal initial guess. Instead, the state-of-the-art for provable optimality relies on relaxing the combinatorial $\ell_{0}$ pseudo-norm into the convex $\ell_{1}$ norm Agarwal et al., (2016) or the convex $\ell_{4}$ norm Zhai et al., (2020). Under assumptions like mutual incoherency Arora et al., (2014), restricted isometry property (RIP) Agarwal et al., (2016) or large sample complexity Sun et al., (2016); Zhai et al., (2020), the relaxation is exact and an optimal solution to the original combinatorial problem can be recovered. However, when the relaxation is inexact, the recovered solution may be drastically different than the solution to the original CDL.

In this paper, we revisit the combinatorial $\ell_{0}$ pseudo-norm in CDL, motivated by the fact that the orthogonal instance (in which the dictionary $\bm{D}$ is constrained to be orthonomal) is significantly easier to analyze. In the orthogonal setting, alternating minimization is simple, in that the minimizations over $\bm{D}$ and $\bm{X}$ at each iteration have simple closed-form solutions. We give the first proof that the resulting sequence converges to the ground truth model under minimal conditions, provided that the algorithm is initialized properly. To extend to general complete dictionaries, which are not necessarily orthogonal, our key idea is to use a data-driven preconditioning step to “orthogonalize” the data. Surprisingly, this preconditioning step allows us to extend our linear convergence guarantee to general complete dictionary learning without significant modifications. As shown in Figure 1, the resulting preconditioned algorithm learns more powerful dictionaries that strike a better balance between the sparsity of representation and the quality of fit, than the commonly-used heuristic KSVD.

### 1.1 Summary of results

At the heart of our method to recover a pair $(\bm{D}^{*},\bm{X}^{*})$ is an efficient alternating minimization algorithm for the orthonormal dictionary learning problem, which reads

$$ \min_{\bm{X},\bm{D}}\|\bm{Y}-\bm{D}\bm{X}\|_{F}^{2}+\zeta\|\bm{X}\|_{0}\quad\text{ s.t. }\bm{D}\in\mathbb{O}(n) $$

where $\mathbb{O}(n)$ denotes the set of $n\times n$ orthonormal matrices. While the orthogonality constraint adds another nonconvex component to the original formulation, we point out that the minimization of $\bm{X}$ for a fixed orthonormal $\bm{D}\in\mathbb{O}(n)$ has a cheap closed-form solution:

$$ \operatorname{argmin}_{\bm{X}}\|\bm{Y}-\bm{D}\bm{X}\|_{F}^{2}+\zeta\|\bm{X}\|_{0}=\mathrm{HT}_{\zeta}(\bm{D}^{T}\bm{Y}) $$

via a hard-thresholding operator $\mathrm{HT}_{\zeta}(\cdot)$ at level $\zeta$ , which is defined as:

$$ \left(\mathrm{HT}_{\zeta}(\bm{A})\right)_{ij}=\begin{cases}\bm{A}_{ij}&\text{if}\quad|\bm{A}_{ij}|\geq\zeta,\\
0&\text{if}\quad|\bm{A}_{ij}|<\zeta.\end{cases} $$

Similarly, the minimization of an orthonormal $\bm{D}\in\mathbb{O}(n)$ for a fixed $\bm{X}$ also has a well-known closed-form solution via the so-called orthogonal Procrustes problem

$$ \underset{\bm{D}\in\mathbb{O}(n)}{\operatorname{argmin}}\ \|\bm{Y}-\bm{D}\bm{X}\|_{F}^{2}+\zeta\|\bm{X}\|_{0}=\mathrm{Polar}(\bm{Y}\bm{X}^{\top}), $$

where $\mathrm{Polar}(\bm{A})=\bm{U}_{\bm{A}}\bm{V}_{\bm{A}}^{\top}$ , and $\bm{U}_{\bm{A}}\bm{\Sigma}_{\bm{A}}\bm{V}_{\bm{A}}^{\top}$ is the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) of $\bm{A}$ . Therefore, the following iterations

$$ \bm{X}^{(t+1)}=\mathrm{HT}_{\zeta}(\bm{D}^{(t)\top}\bm{Y}),\qquad\bm{D}^{(t+1)}=\mathrm{Polar}\left(\bm{Y}\bm{X}^{(t+1)\top}\right) $$

correspond exactly to an alternating minimization solution of Problem ODL. While (1) has been derived before, we give the first rigorous proof that the sequence locally converges at a linear rate with minimal conditions on the sparsity rate of $\bm{X}^{*}$ . Concretely, we prove that when the data are generated as $\bm{Y}=\bm{D}^{*}\bm{X}^{*}$ , with $\bm{D}^{*}$ an orthogonal dictionary, and $\bm{X}^{*}$ a sparse random matrix, (1) converges linearly to a ground truth $(\bm{D}^{*},\bm{X}^{*})$ , when it is initialized within an $O\left(\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{\theta n}}\right)$ Frobenius neighborhood of this solution.

We use a data-driven preconditioning step to generalize (1) to general instances of CDL, for which the square dictionary matrix $\bm{D}^{*}$ is not necessarily orthonormal. The basic idea is to learn an orthonormal dictionary $\tilde{\bm{D}}$ with respect to the preconditioned data matrix $\tilde{\bm{Y}}=(\bm{Y}\bm{Y}^{\top})^{-1/2}\bm{Y}$ , and then to output a complete dictionary $\bm{D}=(\bm{Y}\bm{Y}^{\top})^{+1/2}\tilde{\bm{D}}$ by reversing the preconditioning. Indeed, if the data are generated as $\bm{Y}=\bm{D}^{*}\bm{X}^{*}$ with $\bm{D}^{*}$ deterministic, and $\bm{X}^{*}$ a sparse random matrix satisfying $\mathbb{E}[\bm{X}^{*}\bm{X}^{*\top}]=I_{n}$ , then $\mathbb{E}[\bm{Y}\bm{Y}^{\top}]=\bm{D}^{*}\mathbb{E}[\bm{X}^{*}\bm{X}^{*\top}]\bm{D}^{*\top}=\bm{D}^{*}\bm{D}^{*\top}$ . Therefore, the preconditioned data are generated as $\tilde{\bm{Y}}\approx\tilde{\bm{D}}^{*}\bm{X}^{*}$ with respect to an orthogonal dictionary $\tilde{\bm{D}}^{*}=(\bm{D}^{*}\bm{D}^{*\top})^{+1/2}\bm{D}^{*}$ and the same sparse code $\bm{X}^{*}$ . We show that such preconditioning can be efficiently implemented via low-rank updates of the corresponding Cholesky factors. One of our main contributions is to show that this simple preconditioning step allows us to extend our linear convergence guarantee from orthogonal dictionaries (ODL) to general complete dictionaries (CDL), even in the online and mini-batch settings.

A key strength of our convergence guarantee is that it does not rely on any incoherency/ RIP assumptions. In fact, we can recover very ill-conditioned dictionaries that are highly coherent, although at the expense of a higher sample complexity. Moreover, we can recover codes with sparsity levels in the order of $O(n)$ ; in contrast, existing methods based on alternating minimization can handle sparsity levels of at most $O(n^{\alpha})$ for some $\alpha\leq 1/2$ . Another technique that achieves a near-linear sparsity level $O(n^{1-\gamma})$ for $\gamma>0$ is based on sum-of-squares hierarchy Barak et al., (2015), which is indeed inefficient in practice. Using Riemannian optimization techniques, Sun et al., (2015) was the first to show that CDL with linear sparsity level can be solved in polynomial time. However, the Riemannian optimization algorithm can be expensive, and the associated sample complexity has a dependency of $\Omega(n^{5})$ for orthogonal dictionaries and $\Omega(n^{7})$ for complete dictionaries Sun et al., (2015).

In practice, the iterations (1) admit highly efficient implementations, that can fully take advantage of the massive parallelism inherent in modern hardware. The hard-threshold operator is embarrassingly parallel, while the SVD operation that constitutes the polar operator can be implemented using hardware-optimized LAPACK implementations. The most expensive part of (1) is actually its need to iterate and sum over all $p$ columns of the data matrix $\bm{Y}$ at every iteration. To address potential scalability issues with a very large $p$ , we propose a mini-batch version,

$$ \bm{X}_{(\cdot,i)}^{(t+1)}=\mathrm{HT}_{\zeta}(\bm{D}^{(t)\top}\bm{Y}_{(\cdot,i)})\quad\forall i\in\Omega,\qquad\bm{D}^{(t+1)}=\mathrm{Polar}\left(\sum_{i\in\Omega}\bm{Y}_{(\cdot,i)}\bm{X}_{(\cdot,i)}^{(t+1)\top}\right). $$

that approximates $\bm{Y}\bm{X}^{(t+1)\top}\approx\sum_{i\in\Omega}\bm{Y}_{(\cdot,i)}\bm{X}_{(\cdot,i)}^{(t+1)\top}$ over a mini-batch $\Omega\subseteq\{1,2,\dots,p\}$ , and updates only the sparse codes $\bm{X}_{(\cdot,i)}^{(t+1)}$ associated with the mini-batch samples $i\in\Omega$ . We show that the preconditioner can also be incrementally updated, via an efficient low-rank update formula for the Cholesky factor, which is comparable to the classical Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury formula for updating the determinant/matrix inverse. We show that the accuracy of the recovered dictionary is explicitly lower bounded by the statistical error of the preconditioner. We also show that such an error will diminish in the online setting as more samples come in. This is the first time that efficient updating is applied to methods that use the preconditioning for CDL.

Despite its mini-batch nature, we show that our method enjoys the same sharp linear convergence to the true solution. Finally, we extend our technique to the online dictionary learning, where the data samples arrive sequentially over time. To the best of our knowledge, existing methods for online dictionary learning work with batch sizes of at least $O(n)$ (see e.g. (Rambhatla et al.,, 2019, Theorem 1) and (Arora et al.,, 2015, Theorem 2)). In contrast, our proposed preconditioner admits an efficient triangular rank-one update with as few as one new sample, thereby making it particularly appealing in the online setting.

### 1.2 Related work

#### Optimality conditions

As the first question, we must first verify whether a ground truth $(\bm{D}^{*},\bm{X}^{*})$ is a global minimizer of CDL for the generative model $\bm{Y}=\bm{D}^{*}\bm{X}^{*}$ . Of course, if this were not the case, solving CDL—even to global optimality—may not be enough to recover a ground truth $(\bm{D}^{*},\bm{X}^{*})$ . A series of work Gribonval and Schnass, (2010); Geng and Wright, (2014); Jenatton et al., (2012); Gribonval et al., (2015); Schnass, (2015); Cohen and Gillis, (2019); Hu and Huang, (2023) studied the local optimality of the ground truth for CDL by replacing $\ell_{0}$ norm with $\ell_{1}$ norm. The work Spielman et al., (2012) elegantly showed that the ground truth is the unique global minimizer to CDL when $\zeta\rightarrow 0$ . Specifically, when $p=\Omega(n\log n)$ , they showed that any ground truth $(\bm{D}^{*},\bm{X}^{*})$ is the global minimizer to $\min_{\bm{X},\bm{D}}\|\bm{X}\|_{0}$ subject to the constraint $\bm{Y}=\bm{D}\bm{X}$ . The question remains to be answered: how to design a provable algorithm for recovering $(\bm{X}^{*},\bm{D}^{*})\in\mathcal{M}$ .

#### Alternating minimization

The empirical success achieved by methods like MOD and KSVD has encouraged the emergence of many alternating minimization algorithms Lee et al., (2006); Mairal et al., (2009); Bao et al., (2014). Towards providing a provable guarantee for alternating minimization, it is common to replace the $\ell_{0}$ pseudo-norm with its convex surrogate $\ell_{1}$ norm Agarwal et al., (2016); Chatterji and Bartlett, (2017); Malézieux et al., (2021); Tolooshams and Ba, (2021). Such a compromise is due to the prohibitive computational cost and formidable analytical challenges of $\ell_{0}$ pseudo-norm. However, $\ell_{1}$ relaxation is biased towards solutions with smaller entries, thereby leading to an inferior sparsity level Zhang, (2010). On the algorithmic side, methods based on $\ell_{1}$ relaxation need to solve variants of the LASSO problem at each iteration either exactly Agarwal et al., (2016); Chatterji and Bartlett, (2017) or approximately via an automatic differentiation with backpropagation Malézieux et al., (2021); Tolooshams and Ba, (2021). In this work, we focus on the formulation of CDL without any convex relaxation, which is the original intention of sparse dictionary learning. Unlike the $\ell_{1}$ method, the theoretical underpinnings of the alternating algorithms for the $\ell_{0}$ formulation are far less explored. In Schnass, (2018); Hu and Huang, (2023); Schnass and Teixeira, (2020); Pali and Schnass, (2023), the authors study the convergence behavior of a variant of K-SVD. Specifically, the dictionary update step is performed by maximizing the absolute norm of the $S$ -largest responses where $S$ is the number of non-zero entries in each signal. In Ravishankar et al., (2020), authors propose an alternating scheme based on sorting the non-zero entries of sparse codes. However, the success of these algorithms relies on restrictive generative models like symmetric decaying Schnass, (2015) and fixed sparsity $S$ Ravishankar et al., (2020).

#### Riemannian manifold optimization for complete dictionary learning

One line of work focuses on solving CDL via Riemannian manifold optimization techniques Qu et al., (2014); Zhai et al., (2020). Notably, the work Sun et al., (2016) was the first to show that a smoothed variant of CDL based on $\ell_{1}$ relaxation is devoid of spurious local solutions. Similar benign landscape results have also been independently discovered in the analysis of other problems like matrix factorization Ge et al., (2017). As a result, one can provably recover one dictionary atom at a time via the Riemannian trust-region method. The work Gilboa et al., (2019) showed that similar results can be achieved by first-order methods on the Riemannian manifold. In a different approach, the work Zhai et al., (2020) studied the $\ell_{4}$ maximization on the Steifel manifold, which is further generalized in Shen et al., (2020) to $\ell_{p}$ maximization. Akin to our own work, preconditioning the data matrix plays an important role in these algorithms.

#### Online dictionary learning

Another line of research has focused on the online variants of CDL. The work Mairal et al., (2009) first proposed an online algorithm that solves $\ell_{1}$ relaxation of CDL, but it only guarantees convergence to a critical point. The work Lu et al., (2013) enhanced the usability and practicality of $\ell_{1}$ relaxation but provided no theoretical guarantees. The work Arora et al., (2015) proposed an alternating algorithm that can recover the ground truth $(\bm{X}^{*},\bm{D}^{*})$ , which is further improved in Rambhatla et al., (2019). However, both variants have a specific requirement on the size of the input for each iteration and cannot deal with situations where samples are received one by one.

### 1.3 Notation

We use $\bm{A}_{(i,\cdot)}$ , $\bm{A}_{(\cdot,j)}$ and $\bm{A}_{ij}$ to denote the $i$ th row, $j$ th column and $(i,j)$ -th entry of $\bm{A}$ , respectively. We use $\|\bm{A}\|_{2}$ to denote the spectral norm of $\bm{A}$ , $\|\bm{A}\|_{F}$ to denote Frobenius norm of $\bm{A}$ , $\|\bm{A}\|_{1,2}$ to denote the maximum $2$ -norm of the columns of $\bm{A}$ , $\|\bm{A}\|_{0}$ to denote the total number of non-zero entries in $\bm{A}$ , and $\|\bm{A}\|_{1}$ to denote the entry-wise $\ell_{1}$ norm of $\bm{A}$ . The symbol $\bm{I}_{d}$ denotes the $d\times d$ identity matrix, and $\mathbb{O}(n)$ denotes the orthogonal group in dimension $n$ . We use $\mathrm{supp}(\bm{A})$ to refer to the set of indices of non-zero entries of $\bm{A}$ . The symbol $\sigma_{i}(\bm{A})$ denotes the $i$ th largest singular value of $\bm{A}$ and $\kappa(\bm{A})$ denotes the condition number of $\bm{A}$ . Given a matrix $\bm{A}$ , its polar decomposition is defined as $\mathrm{Polar}(\bm{A})=\bm{U}_{\bm{A}}\bm{V}_{\bm{A}}^{\top}$ , where $\bm{U}_{\bm{A}}\bm{\Sigma}_{\bm{A}}\bm{V}_{\bm{A}}^{\top}$ is the SVD of $\bm{A}$ . We also define the operator $\mathcal{L}(\bm{A})=\bm{L}_{\bm{A}}^{\top}$ , where $\bm{L}_{\bm{A}}\bm{L}_{\bm{A}}^{\top}$ is the Cholesky factorization of a positive semidefinite matrix $\bm{A}$ . For an event $\mathcal{E}$ , its indicator function is denoted as $\mathbbm{1}_{\mathcal{E}}$ . Given two sequences $f(n)$ and $g(n)$ , the notations $f(n)\lesssim g(n)$ and $f(n)=O(g(n))$ imply that there exists a universal constant $C>0$ satisfying $f(n)\leq Cg(n)$ for all large enough $n$ . Similarly, the notations $f(n)\gtrsim g(n)$ and $f(n)=\Omega(g(n))$ imply that there exists a universal constant $C>0$ satisfying $f(n)\geq Cg(n)$ for all large enough $n$ . We use $f(n)=\omega(g(n))$ if for all constants $C>0$ we have $f(n)\geq Cg(n)$ for all large enough $n$ . We say an event happens with high probability if it occurs with probability of at least $1-n^{-\omega(1)}$ with respect to all randomness in the problem.

## 2 Our Method

We consider a noiseless model, where the data matrix is generated according to $\bm{Y}=\bm{D}^{*}\bm{X}^{*}$ . For any signed permutation matrix $\Pi$ , the pair $(\bm{D}^{*}\Pi,\Pi^{\top}\bm{X}^{*})$ is also a valid ground truth that satisfies $\left\lVert\Pi^{\top}\bm{X}^{*}\right\rVert_{0}=\left\lVert\bm{X}^{*}\right\rVert_{0}$ .11 1 A signed permutation matrix is a generalized permutation matrix whose nonzero entries are $\pm 1$ . Let $\mathcal{M}=\{(\bm{D}^{*}\Pi,\Pi^{\top}\bm{X}^{*}):\text{$\Pi$ is a signed permutation}\}$ . Our goal is to recover an arbitrary element $(\bm{D}^{*}\Pi,\Pi^{\top}\bm{X}^{*})\in\mathcal{M}$ .

### 2.1 Orthogonal Dictionary Learning

We first assume that the dictionary is an orthogonal matrix $\bm{D}^{*}\in\mathbb{O}(n)$ . This leads to the following alternating minimization algorithm based on the closed-form solutions (1):

*Algorithm 1 Alternating minimization for ODL*

```
1: Input: $\bm{Y}$ , $\bm{D}^{(0)}$ , $\zeta$
2: for $t=0,1,\dots,T$ do
3: Set $\bm{X}^{(t)}=\mathrm{HT}_{\zeta}\left(\bm{D}^{(t)\top}\bm{Y}\right)$
4: Set $\bm{D}^{(t+1)}=\mathrm{Polar}\left(\bm{Y}\bm{X}^{(t)\top}\right)$
5: end for
6: return $\bm{D}^{(T)}$ , $\bm{X}^{(T)}$
```

We note that Algorithm 1 has been studied before. The paper Bao et al., (2013) reports the empirical performance of Algorithm 1 on an image restoration task. The paper Ravishankar et al., (2020) provides a theoretical analysis for a variant of Algorithm 1 based on sorted thresholding. One may even argue that Algorithm 1 is similar to the Method of Optimal Directions (MOD). However, the existing theoretical guarantees for Algorithm 1 are indeed restrictive (see the discussion on alternating minimization in Section 1.2). To bridge this knowledge gap, we first introduce our assumption on the sparse matrix $\bm{X}$ .

#### Assumption 1 (Model for sparse code).

The sparsity pattern of ground truth $\bm{X}^{*}$ follows a Bernoulli distribution with parameter $\theta=(0,1]$ . In particular,

$$ \mathbbm{1}_{\bm{X}^{*}_{ij}\neq 0}=B_{ij},\quad\text{where}\quad B_{ij}\overset{i.i.d.}{\sim}\mathcal{B}(\theta)\text{ for all $1\leq i\leq n$, $1\leq j\leq p$}. $$

The non-zero values of $\bm{X}^{*}$ are independently drawn from a sub-Gaussian distribution with mean zero and constant variance $\sigma^{2}$ . Moreover, the magnitudes of non-zero entries of $\bm{X}^{*}$ are lower bounded by some constant $\Gamma$ . More specifically, we have

$$ |\bm{X}^{*}_{ij}|\geq\Gamma,\quad\mathbb{E}(\bm{X}^{*}_{ij})=0,\quad\text{and}\quad\mathbb{E}(\bm{X}^{*2}_{ij})=\sigma^{2},\text{ for every $(i,j)\in\mathrm{supp}(\bm{X}^{*})$.} $$

Now, we are ready to show the convergence of Algorithm 1:

#### Theorem 1.

Suppose that $\bm{Y}=\bm{D}^{*}\bm{X}^{*}$ where $\bm{D}^{*}$ is orthogonal and $\bm{X}^{*}$ satisfies Assumption 1 with sparsity level $0<\theta<1/2$ . Suppose that the initial dictionary $\bm{D}^{(0)}$ satisfies $\|\bm{D}^{(0)}-\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F}\lesssim\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{\theta n}}$ for some $(\bm{D}^{*},\bm{X}^{*})\in\mathcal{M}$ . Moreover, suppose that $n/\theta^{2}\lesssim p\lesssim n^{\gamma}$ for some constant $\gamma>0$ . Then, with probability at least $1-n^{-\omega(1)}$ , for any $T\geq 1$ , the output of Algorithm 1 with $\zeta=\Gamma/2$ satisfies:

$$ \displaystyle\|\bm{D}^{(T)}-\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F}\leq 0.9^{T}\|\bm{D}^{(0)}-\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F},\quad\|\bm{X}^{(T)}-\bm{X}^{*}\|_{F}\leq 0.9^{T}\|\bm{X}^{(0)}-\bm{X}^{*}\|_{F} $$

Theorem 1 improves upon the existing results on two fronts:

#### Linear sparsity level

We allow a constant fraction of entries in $\bm{X}^{*}$ to be non-zero, thereby improving upon the best known sparsity level of $O(\sqrt{n}/\log n)$ for alternating minimization Arora et al., (2015). Moreover, the imposed upper bound on the sample size asserts that it must be bounded by a polynomial function of $n$ . This mild assumption is only included to simplify the presentation of our main result.

#### Linear sample complexity

In order to recover $\bm{D}^{*}$ exactly, we only need to observe $O(n)$ many samples, which is $\log(n)$ factor smaller than the sample complexity required for the uniqueness of the solution when $\xi\rightarrow 0$ Spielman et al., (2012). This sample complexity is optimal (modulo constant factors) since it is impossible to recover the true dictionary with a sublinear number of samples even if $\bm{X}^{*}$ is known. Note that the theoretical convergence of Algorithm 1 is contingent upon a good initial dictionary. As shown in Lemma 1, the imposed condition on the initial dictionary automatically guarantees the recovery of the support for any $\bm{X}^{(t)}$ with $t\geq 0$ . In Subsection 2.4, we discuss possible ways to obtain such an initial dictionary in theory and practice. We also suspect that our initialization requirement can be improved to $\|\bm{D}^{(0)}-\bm{D}^{*}\|_{1,2}\leq O(1/\log n)$ with fresh samples at every iteration, which is the best-known radius for alternating minimization Arora et al., (2015).

Despite its desirable properties, Algorithm 1 suffers from two fundamental limitations. First, its convergence depends on the orthogonality of the true dictionary, which may not be satisfied in many applications. Second, it does not readily extend to huge-scale or online settings, where it is prohibitive or even impossible to process all data samples together. To address these challenges, we next extend our algorithm to complete (non-orthogonal) dictionary learning with mini-batch and online data.

### 2.2 Mini-batch Complete Dictionary Learning

To distinguish from ODL, we denote the ground truth dictionary as $\bm{A}^{*}$ (i.e., $\bm{Y}=\bm{A}^{*}\bm{X}^{*}$ ). Towards dealing with large $p$ , we sub-sample from the columns of $\bm{Y}$ . To address the non-orthogonality of the dictionary, we consider a preconditioner $\bm{P}$ defined as

$$ \bm{P}=\mathcal{L}\left(\left(\frac{1}{p\theta\sigma^{2}}\bm{Y}\bm{Y}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\right). $$

Using this preconditioner, we obtain a new (preconditioned) data matrix $\tilde{\bm{Y}}=\bm{P}\bm{Y}$ . To explain the intuition behind this choice of preconditioner, note that $\frac{1}{p\theta\sigma^{2}}\bm{Y}\bm{Y}^{\top}\approx\bm{A}^{*}\bm{A}^{*\top}$ for large enough $p$ , which allows us to write $\tilde{\bm{Y}}\approx\mathcal{L}\left(\left(\bm{A}^{*}\bm{A}^{*\top}\right)^{-1}\right)\bm{A}^{*}\bm{X}^{*}$ . Upon defining $\bm{D}^{*}=\mathcal{L}\left(\left(\bm{A}^{*}\bm{A}^{*\top}\right)^{-1}\right)\bm{A}^{*}$ , one can check that $\bm{D}^{*}\in\mathbb{O}(n)$ and $\tilde{\bm{Y}}\approx\bm{D}^{*}\bm{X}^{*}$ . Indeed, this is an instance of ODL and can be solved via Algorithm 1. The detailed implementation is provided in Algorithm 2. We note that the dependency of the preconditioner on $\theta$ and $\sigma^{2}$ is purely to simplify the presentation and can be replaced by a simple normalization step in practice.

*Algorithm 2 Alternating minimization for mini-batch CDL*

```
1: Input: $\bm{Y}$ , $\bm{A}^{(0)}$ , $\zeta$
2: Set $\bm{P}\!=\!\mathcal{L}\left(\left(\frac{1}{p\theta\sigma^{2}}\bm{Y}\bm{Y}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\right)^{\top}$ ,​ $\tilde{\bm{Y}}\!=\!\bm{P}\bm{Y}$ , and $\bm{D}^{(0)}\!=\!\bm{P}\bm{A}^{(0)}$ .
3: for $t=0,1,\dots,T-1$ do
4: Sample $\tilde{p}$ many columns from $\tilde{\bm{Y}}$ to be $\tilde{\bm{Y}}^{(t)}$ .
5: Set $\tilde{\bm{X}}^{(t)}=\mathrm{HT}_{\zeta}\left(\bm{D}^{(t)\top}\tilde{\bm{Y}}^{(t)}\right)$ .
6: Set $\bm{D}^{(t+1)}=\mathrm{Polar}\left(\tilde{\bm{Y}}^{(t)}\tilde{\bm{X}}^{(t)\top}\right)$ .
7: end for
8: return $\bm{A}^{(T)}=\bm{P}^{-1}\bm{D}^{(T)}$ as an approximation to $\bm{A}^{*}$
```

Our next theorem characterizes the performance of Algorithm 2.

Without loss of generality, we assume that $\|\bm{A}^{*}\|_{2}=1$ and set $\hat{\kappa}$ to be the condition number of $\bm{A}^{*}$ .

#### Theorem 2.

Suppose that $\bm{Y}=\bm{A}^{*}\bm{X}^{*}$ , where $\bm{X}^{*}$ satisfies Assumption 1 with sparsity level $0<\theta<1/2$ . Suppose that the initial dictionary $\bm{A}^{(0)}$ satisfies $\|\bm{A}^{(0)}-\bm{A}^{*}\|_{F}\lesssim\frac{1}{\hat{\kappa}\sigma\sqrt{\theta n}}$ for some $(\bm{A}^{*},\bm{X}^{*})\in\mathcal{M}$ . Moreover, suppose that $n/\theta^{2}\lesssim\tilde{p}\lesssim n^{\gamma}$ , $\hat{\kappa}^{12}n^{3}\log^{2}\tilde{p}/\theta\lesssim p$ , $T\lesssim n^{\beta}$ and $\log n\gtrsim\beta+\gamma$ , for some constants $\gamma,\beta>0$ . Then with probability at least $1-n^{-\omega(1)}$ , the output of Algorithm 2 with $\zeta=\Gamma/2$ satisfies:

$$ \displaystyle\left\|\bm{A}^{(T)}-\bm{A}^{*}\right\|_{F}\leq \displaystyle\ 0.9^{T}\|\bm{A}^{(0)}-\bm{A}^{*}\|_{F}+O\left(\frac{n\hat{\kappa}^{6}}{\theta\sqrt{p}}\right). $$

Theorem 2 states that Algorithm 2 converges linearly to the true dictionary up to a statistical error $O\left(\frac{n\hat{\kappa}^{6}}{\theta\sqrt{p}}\right)$ . This statistical error is due to the deviation of the preconditioner from its expectation, which diminishes with $p$ . A key distinction of our result is that we do not impose any incoherency requirement or restricted isometry property on $\bm{A}^{*}$ , which are common assumptions in existing results. We also highlight that the upper bound on $T$ is indeed very mild. To demonstrate this, note that, in order to guarantee $0.9^{T}\left\lVert\mathbf{A}^{(0)}-\mathbf{A}^{*}\right\rVert_{F}=O\left(\frac{n\hat{\kappa}^{6}}{\theta\sqrt{p}}\right)$ , it suffices to have $T=\Omega\left(\frac{\theta\sqrt{p}}{\hat{\kappa}^{6}n\log n}\right)$ , a condition that satisfies $T=O(n^{\beta})$ for some $\beta>0$ for all practical purposes.

### 2.3 Online Dictionary Learning

Even though the computational efficiency of Algorithm 2 is largely improved compared to its full-batch counterpart, it may not be implementable in huge-scale or online settings due to the dependency of the preconditioner on the entire dataset with size $p$ . Both situations call for a cheap method to update the preconditioner more efficiently in an online fashion.

To update $\bm{P}$ with a new sample $\bm{y}$ , a naive approach would be to re-compute it from scratch which would cost $O(n^{3})$ operations. However, we show that $\bm{P}$ can be updated more efficiently in $O(n^{2})$ operations by taking advantage of the more efficient rank-one updates on matrix inversion and Cholesky factorization. To this goal, we first use the Sherman-Morrison formula to update $\left(\bm{Y}\bm{Y}^{\top}\right)^{-1}$ as

$$ \displaystyle\left(\bm{Y}\bm{Y}^{\top}\!+\!\bm{y}\bm{y}^{\top}\right)^{-1}= \displaystyle\left(\bm{Y}\bm{Y}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\!-\!\bm{v}\bm{v}^{\top},\ \ \text{where}\ \ \bm{v}=\left(1+\bm{y}^{\top}\left(\bm{Y}\bm{Y}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\bm{y}\right)^{-1/2}\left(\bm{Y}\bm{Y}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\bm{y}, $$

which, given $\left(\bm{Y}\bm{Y}^{\top}\right)^{-1}$ , can be obtained in $O(n^{2})$ operations. Given the above rank-one update for the inverse, the Cholesky factor $\mathcal{L}\left(\left(\bm{Y}\bm{Y}^{\top}+\bm{y}\bm{y}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\right)$ can be obtained within $O(n^{2})$ operations by performing triangular rank-one updates on $\mathcal{L}\left(\left(\bm{Y}\bm{Y}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\right)$ Krause and Igel, (2015). We explain the implementation of this method in Appendix C.

Inspired by the above update, we propose an online variant of Algorithm 3. We start the algorithm by initializing the preconditioner and the data matrix using $p_{1}$ and $p_{2}$ samples, respectively, both potentially significantly smaller than $p$ . When a new sample arrives, we update the preconditioner $\bm{P}^{(t)}$ via the triangular rank-one update and update the data set accordingly.

*Algorithm 3 Alternating minimization for online dictionary learning*

```
1: Input: $\bm{A}^{(0)}$ , $\zeta$ , $p_{1}$ , $p_{2}$
2: Set $\bm{Z}^{(0)}_{\text{inv}}=\left(\bar{\bm{Y}}\bar{\bm{Y}}^{\top}\right)^{-1}$ , $\bm{P}^{(0)}=\mathcal{L}\left({p_{1}\theta\sigma^{2}}\bm{Z}^{(0)}_{\text{inv}}\right)^{\top}$ , where $\bar{\bm{Y}}$ is constructed with $p_{1}$ samples and $\bm{D}^{(0)}\!=\!\bm{P}^{(0)}\bm{A}^{(0)}$ .
3: Initialize $\bm{Y}^{(0)}$ with $p_{2}$ samples.
4: for $t=0,1,\dots,T-1$ do
5: Given a new $\bm{y}$ , set $\bm{Y}^{(t)}\!\!=\!\![\bm{Y}^{(t-1)}\ \bm{y}]$ and remove the first column of $\bm{Y}^{(t)}$ .
6: Update $\bm{P}^{(t)}$ and $\bm{Z}^{(t)}_{\text{inv}}$ using $\bm{P}^{(t-1)}$ , $\bm{Z}^{(t-1)}_{\text{inv}}$ , and $\bm{y}$ via Algorithm 5.
7: Set $\tilde{\bm{Y}}^{(t)}=\bm{P}^{(t)}\bm{Y}^{(t)}$
8: Set $\tilde{\bm{X}}^{(t)}=\mathrm{HT}_{\zeta}\left(\bm{D}^{(t)\top}\tilde{\bm{Y}}^{(t)}\right)$ .
9: Set $\bm{D}^{(t+1)}=\mathrm{Polar}\left(\tilde{\bm{Y}}^{(t)}\tilde{\bm{X}}^{(t)\top}\right)$ .
10: end for
11: return $\left(\bm{P}^{(T-1)}\right)^{-1}\bm{D}^{(T)}$ as an approximation to $\bm{A}^{*}$
```

Our next theorem establishes the convergence of Algorithm 3.

#### Theorem 3.

Suppose that $\bm{Y}=\bm{A}^{*}\bm{X}^{*}$ , where $\bm{X}^{*}$ satisfies Assumption 1 with sparsity level $0<\theta<1/2$ . Suppose that the initial dictionary $\bm{A}^{(0)}$ satisfies $\|\bm{A}^{(0)}\!-\!\bm{A}^{*}\|_{F}\lesssim\frac{1}{\hat{\kappa}\sigma\sqrt{\theta n}}$ for some $(\bm{A}^{*},\bm{X}^{*})\in\mathcal{M}$ . Moreover, suppose that $n/\theta^{2}\lesssim p_{2}\lesssim n^{\gamma}$ , $\hat{\kappa}^{12}n^{3}\log^{2}p_{2}/\theta\lesssim p_{1}$ and $T\lesssim n^{\beta}$ , for some constants $\gamma,\beta>0$ . Then, with probability at least $1-n^{-\omega(1)}$ , the output of Algorithm 3 with $\zeta=\Gamma/2$ satisfies:

$$ \displaystyle\left\|\bm{A}^{(T)}-\bm{A}^{*}\right\|_{F}\leq \displaystyle\ 0.9^{T}\|\bm{A}^{(0)}-\bm{A}^{*}\|_{F}+O\left(\frac{n\hat{\kappa}^{6}}{\theta\sqrt{p_{1}+T}}\right). $$

The convergence result of Algorithm 3 is similar to that of Algorithm 2, with a key difference that the statistical error $O\left(\frac{n\hat{\kappa}^{6}}{\theta\sqrt{p_{1}+T}}\right)$ now decreases with $T$ , which is due to the fact that the preconditioner becomes progressively more accurate as new samples continue to arrive.

### 2.4 Initialization

The theoretical success of Algorithms 1-3 requires, at least in theory, a good initialization with $O(1/\sqrt{\theta n})$ distance to the ground truth. Such initialization can be provided by the initialization scheme introduced in Agarwal et al., (2016) and Arora et al., (2015), albeit with slightly more restrictive conditions on the sparsity level. For the same generative model as described in Assumption 1, computationally intensive and data-intensive algorithms, such as the Riemannian Trust Region method (RTR) Sun et al., (2015), can also be employed to design initial dictionaries that satisfy the conditions outlined in Theorems 1-3. Specifically, for ODL, (Sun et al.,, 2015, Theorem 3.1) demonstrates that the RTR can obtain an initial point with a distance of $O(1/\sqrt{\theta n})$ from the ground truth, albeit with an increased sample complexity of $p=\Omega(n^{5})$ . Similarly, for CDL, (Sun et al.,, 2015, Theorem 3.2) illustrates that RTR can yield an initial point with a distance of $O(1/\sqrt{\theta n})$ from the ground truth with a sample complexity of $p=\Omega(n^{7})$ . Combining these results with Theorems 1-3 allows for an end-to-end global guarantee at the cost of increasing the sample complexity to $\Omega(n^{5})$ for ODL and $\Omega(n^{7})$ for CDL.

However, we note that these tailored initialization schemes are not easily implementable, especially in a huge-scale regime. In practice, we observed that a simple warm-start algorithm would yield similar performance. Consider a variant of Algorithm 1 with a diminishing threshold presented in Algorithm 4 (the warm-start schemes for Algorithms 2 and 3 are similar and hence omitted for brevity).

Notice that a large $\zeta_{0}$ will force $\bm{X}^{(t)}$ to be an all-zero matrix and make $\bm{D}^{(t+1)}$ an identity matrix. As we shrink the threshold $\zeta_{t}$ , the matrix $\bm{X}^{(t)}$ eventually becomes nonzero, and the iterates $\bm{D}^{(0)}$ start to gradually move towards the basin of attraction of $\bm{D}^{*}$ . Figure 2 demonstrates how our proposed warm-start algorithm generates an initial dictionary that is sufficiently close to the true dictionary. We also observe that, in practice, the convergence of iterates from $\bm{I}_{d}$ to the basin of local convergence is not linear. However, once the iterates reach this basin, they exhibit linear convergence to the ground truth, which is theoretically guaranteed by Theorem 1. We also note that our proposed warm-start algorithm can serve as an effective initialization scheme for other DL algorithms, including those discussed in Section 1.2. The theoretical analysis of this warm-start algorithm is left as an enticing challenge for future research.

*Algorithm 4 Algorithm 1 with warm-start*

```
1: Input: $\bm{Y}$ , $\zeta_{0}$ , $\zeta$ , $\beta\in(0,1)$
2: Set $\bm{D}^{(0)}=\bm{I}_{n}$
3: for $t=0,1,\dots,T_{0}$ do
4: $\zeta_{t+1}=\max\{\beta\zeta_{t},\zeta\}$
5: Set $\bm{X}^{(t)}=\mathrm{HT}_{\zeta_{t}}\left(\bm{D}^{(t)\top}\bm{Y}\right)$
6: Set $\bm{D}^{(t+1)}=\bm{I}_{n}$ if $\bm{X}^{(t)}=\mathbf{0}_{n}$ , and $\bm{D}^{(t+1)}=\mathrm{Polar}\left(\bm{Y}\bm{X}^{(t)\top}\right)$ if $\bm{X}^{(t)}\not=\mathbf{0}_{n}$ .
7: end for
8: return $\bm{D}^{(T_{0})}$
```

## 3 Proofs

In this section, we present the proofs of our main theorems.

### 3.1 Proof of Theorem 1

We use induction to prove Theorem 1. We consider the following induction hypothesis:

$$ \|\bm{D}^{(s)}-\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F}=O\left(\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{\theta n}}\right)\qquad\text{at iteration $s$.} $$

As will be shown later, this induction hypothesis will lead to the desired linear convergence result. The base case is verified, given the initial condition. We next present the following two key lemmas, the proofs of which can be found in Appendix B.

#### Lemma 1 (Exact support recovery).

Consider $\bm{Y}=\bm{D}^{*}\bm{X}^{*}$ where $\bm{D}^{*}\in\mathbb{O}^{n}$ and $\bm{X}^{*}$ satisfies Assumption 1. For all $\bm{D}$ satisfying $\|\bm{D}-\bm{D}^{*}\|_{1,2}=O\left(\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{\theta n}}\right)$ , with probability at least $1-2\exp\left(\log p-Cn\right)$ , we have $\mathrm{supp}\left(\mathrm{HT}_{\Gamma/2}\left(\bm{D}^{\top}\bm{Y}\right)\right)=\mathrm{supp}\left(\bm{X}^{*}\right)$ .

#### Lemma 2 (Guaranteed improvement on polar decomposition).

Consider $\bm{Y}=\bm{D}^{*}\bm{X}^{*}$ where $\bm{D}^{*}\in\mathbb{O}^{n}$ and $\bm{X}^{*}$ satisfies Assumption 1 with sparsity level $0<\theta<1/2$ and suppose that $p=\Omega\left(n/\theta^{2}\right)$ . Then, with probability at least $1-2\exp(\log n-n)$ , the following inequality holds for every approximation $\bm{X}$ of $\bm{X}^{*}$ such that $\frac{\|\bm{X}-\bm{X}^{*}\|_{F}}{\|\bm{X}^{*}\|_{2}}=O(1)$ and $\mathrm{supp}(\bm{X})=\mathrm{supp}(\bm{X}^{*})$ :

$$ \|\mathrm{Polar}(\bm{Y}\bm{X}^{\top})-\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F}<0.9\frac{\|\bm{X}-\bm{X}^{*}\|_{F}}{\|\bm{X}^{*}\|_{2}}. $$

Lemma 1 together with our induction hypothesis (5) implies that

$$ \mathrm{supp}\left(\bm{X}^{(s)}\right)=\mathrm{supp}\left(\mathrm{HT}_{\Gamma/2}(\bm{D}^{(s)\top}\bm{Y})\right)=\mathrm{supp}\left(\bm{X}^{*}\right). $$

We can use the exact recovery of support to bound the error on the sparse code:

$$ \displaystyle\|\bm{X}^{(s)}-\bm{X}^{*}\|_{F} \displaystyle=\|\mathrm{HT}_{\Gamma/2}(\bm{D}^{(s)\top}\bm{Y})-\bm{X}^{*}\|_{F}\overset{(a)}{\leq}\|\bm{D}^{(s)}-\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F}\|\bm{Y}\|_{2}, $$

where we used (6) for (a). The above inequality implies that

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\|\bm{X}^{(s)}-\bm{X}^{*}\|_{F}}{\|\bm{X}^{*}\|_{2}} \displaystyle=\frac{\|\bm{X}^{(s)}-\bm{X}^{*}\|_{F}}{\|\bm{D}^{*}\bm{X}^{*}\|_{2}}=\frac{\|\bm{X}^{(s)}-\bm{X}^{*}\|_{F}}{\|\bm{Y}\|_{2}}\leq\|\bm{D}^{(s)}-\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F}=O\left(\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{\theta n}}\right) $$

Invoking Lemma 2 with $\bm{X}=\bm{X}^{(s)}$ together with (7) leads to

$$ \|\bm{D}^{(s+1)}-\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F}<\frac{0.9\|\bm{X}^{(s)}-\bm{X}^{*}\|_{F}}{\|\bm{X}^{*}\|_{2}}<0.9\|\bm{D}^{(s)}-\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F}. $$

Therefore, the induction hypothesis (5) holds for $t=s+1$ . Consequently, the linear convergence for $\frac{\|\bm{X}^{(s)}-\bm{X}^{*}\|_{F}}{\|\bm{X}^{*}\|_{2}}$ follows from (7) and the above inequality:

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\|\bm{X}^{(s+1)}-\bm{X}^{*}\|_{F}}{\|\bm{X}^{*}\|_{2}} \displaystyle\leq\|\bm{D}^{(s+1)}-\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F}<0.9\frac{\|\bm{X}^{(s)}-\bm{X}^{*}\|_{F}}{\|\bm{X}^{*}\|_{2}}. $$

The proof is complete by noticing a lower bound of the probability that both Lemma 1 and Lemma 2 hold is $1-2\exp\left(\log p-Cn\right)-2\exp(\log n-n)=1-n^{-\omega(1)}$ , which follows from our assumption $p=O(n^{\gamma})$ . This completes the proof. $\hfill\square$

Next, we provide the proof of Theorem 3. As will be shown later, the proof of Theorem 2 readily follows from this proof.

### 3.2 Proof of Theorem 3

The linear convergence of $\bm{A}^{(T)}$ hinges on the linear convergence of the preconditioned dictionary $\bm{D}^{(T)}$ towards

$$ \bm{D}^{*}=\mathcal{L}((\bm{A}^{*}\bm{A}^{*\top})^{-1})^{\top}\bm{A}^{*}. $$

To establish this fact, we first prove the following inequality:

$$ \displaystyle\|\bm{D}^{(s+1)}-\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F}\leq 0.9\|\bm{D}^{(s)}-\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F}+O\left(\|\bm{P}^{(s)}\bm{A}^{*}-\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F}\right),\quad s=0,2,\dots,T-1 $$

We present the following intermediate lemmas, the proofs of which are in Appendix B.

#### Lemma 3 (Bounding preconditioner error).

Suppose that $\bm{X}^{*}$ satisfies Assumption 1. Then, with probability at least $1-2\exp(-n)$ , we have:

$$ \left\|\bm{P}^{(t)}-\mathcal{L}\left(\left(\bm{A}^{*}\bm{A}^{*\top}\right)^{-1}\right)^{\top}\right\|_{2}\leq O\left(\frac{\hat{\kappa}^{6}}{\theta}\sqrt{\frac{n}{p_{1}+t}}\right). $$

#### Lemma 4 (Spectral property for sparse code matrix).

Suppose that $\bm{X}^{*}$ satisfies Assumption 1 and $p=\Omega(\tau n/\theta^{2})$ for an arbitrary $\tau>0$ . Then, with probability at least $1-2\exp(-n)$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\|\bm{X}^{*}\|_{2}\leq\left(1+\tau^{-\frac{1}{4}}\right) \displaystyle\sqrt{p\theta}\sigma,\quad\sigma_{n}\left(\bm{X}^{*}\right)\geq\left(1-\tau^{-\frac{1}{4}}\right)\sqrt{p\theta}\sigma,\quad\kappa\left(\bm{X}^{*}\right)\leq\frac{1+\tau^{-\frac{1}{4}}}{1-\tau^{-\frac{1}{4}}}. $$

Similar with the proof of Theorem 2, we will use the induction hypothesis $\|\bm{D}^{(s)}-\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F}\leq O\left(\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{\theta n}}\right)$ . The base case is easy to verify given the initial condition and Lemma 3:

$$ \displaystyle\quad\|\bm{D}^{(0)}-\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F}=\|\bm{P}^{(0)}\bm{A}^{(0)}-\mathcal{L}((\bm{A}^{*}\bm{A}^{*\top})^{-1})^{\top}\bm{A}^{*}\|_{F} \displaystyle=\|\bm{P}^{(0)}\bm{A}^{(0)}-\mathcal{L}((\bm{A}^{*}\bm{A}^{*\top})^{-1})^{\top}\bm{A}^{(0)}+\mathcal{L}((\bm{A}^{*}\bm{A}^{*\top})^{-1})^{\top}\bm{A}^{(0)}-\mathcal{L}((\bm{A}^{*}\bm{A}^{*\top})^{-1})^{\top}\bm{A}^{*}\|_{F} \displaystyle\leq\|\bm{P}^{(0)}-\mathcal{L}((\bm{A}^{*}\bm{A}^{*\top})^{-1})^{\top}\|_{2}\|\bm{A}^{(0)}\|_{F}+\|\mathcal{L}((\bm{A}^{*}\bm{A}^{*\top})^{-1})^{\top}\|_{2}\|\bm{A}^{(0)}-\bm{A}^{*}\|_{F} \displaystyle\leq O\left(\frac{\hat{\kappa}^{6}}{\theta}\sqrt{\frac{n}{p_{1}}}\cdot\sqrt{n}\right)+O\left(\hat{\kappa}\cdot\frac{1}{\hat{\kappa}\sigma\sqrt{\theta n}}\right)=O\left(\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{\theta n}}\right). $$

Moreover, after achieving (8) for each $s$ , we have $\|\bm{D}^{(s+1)}-\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F}=O\left(\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{\theta n}}\right)$ since

$$ \|\bm{P}^{(s)}\bm{A}^{*}-\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F}\leq\left\|\bm{P}^{(s)}-\mathcal{L}\left(\left(\bm{A}^{*}\bm{A}^{*\top}\right)^{-1}\right)^{\top}\right\|_{2}\|\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F}=O\left(\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{\theta n}}\right). $$

For the remainder of this section, we abuse the notation and use $\bm{X}^{*}$ to denote the sparse code that generates $\bm{Y}^{(s)}=\bm{A}^{*}\bm{X}^{*}$ , where $\bm{Y}^{(s)}$ is obtained by adding the latest sample as the last column and removing the oldest sample from its first column (see Steps 6 and 7 in Algorithm 3). We also define $\tilde{\bm{X}}$ as $\tilde{\bm{X}}=\bm{D}^{*\top}\tilde{\bm{Y}}^{(s)}$ , which is again a different sparse code for different iterations since $\tilde{\bm{Y}}^{(s)}=\bm{P}^{(s)}\bm{Y}^{(s)}$ and both $\bm{P}^{(s)}$ and $\bm{Y}^{(s)}$ change from iteration to iteration. So far, we have upper bounded $\frac{\|\tilde{\bm{X}}^{(s)}-\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})\|_{F}}{\|\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})\|_{2}}$ with $\|\bm{D}^{(s)}-\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F}$ . Next, we provide an upper bound on $\|\bm{D}^{(s+1)}-\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F}$ in terms of $\frac{\|\tilde{\bm{X}}^{(s)}-\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})\|_{F}}{\|\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})\|_{2}}$ . We have

$$ \displaystyle\|\bm{D}^{(s+1)}-\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F}=\|\mathrm{Polar}(\tilde{\bm{Y}}^{(s)}\tilde{\bm{X}}^{(s)\top})-\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F}=\ \|\mathrm{Polar}(\bm{D}^{*}\tilde{\bm{X}}\tilde{\bm{X}}^{(s)\top})-\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F} \displaystyle=\|\mathrm{Polar}(\bm{D}^{*}\tilde{\bm{X}}\tilde{\bm{X}}^{(s)\top})-\mathrm{Polar}(\bm{D}^{*}\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})\tilde{\bm{X}}^{(s)\top})+\mathrm{Polar}(\bm{D}^{*}\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})\tilde{\bm{X}}^{(s)\top})-\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F} \displaystyle=\|\mathrm{Polar}(\bm{D}^{*}\tilde{\bm{X}}\tilde{\bm{X}}^{(s)\top})\!-\!\mathrm{Polar}(\bm{D}^{*}\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})\tilde{\bm{X}}^{(s)\top})\|_{F}\!+\!\|\mathrm{Polar}(\bm{D}^{*}\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})\tilde{\bm{X}}^{(s)\top})\!-\!\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F} $$

To control the first term on the right-hand side, we invoke Theorem 6 (see Appendix A):

$$ \displaystyle\|\mathrm{Polar}(\bm{D}^{*}\tilde{\bm{X}}\tilde{\bm{X}}^{(s)\top})-\mathrm{Polar}(\bm{D}^{*}\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})\tilde{\bm{X}}^{(s)\top})\|_{F} \displaystyle\leq\  \displaystyle\frac{2\|\bm{D}^{*}\tilde{\bm{X}}\tilde{\bm{X}}^{(s)\top}-\bm{D}^{*}\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})\tilde{\bm{X}}^{(s)\top}\|_{F}}{\sigma_{n}(\bm{D}^{*}\tilde{\bm{X}}\tilde{\bm{X}}^{(s)\top})+\sigma_{n}(\bm{D}^{*}\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})\tilde{\bm{X}}^{(s)\top})} \displaystyle\overset{(a)}{\leq}\  \displaystyle\frac{2\kappa(\tilde{\bm{X}}^{(s)})\|\tilde{\bm{X}}-\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})\|_{F}}{2\sigma_{n}(\bm{X}^{*})-\|\bm{X}^{*}-\tilde{\bm{X}}\|_{2}-\|\bm{X}^{*}-\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})\|_{2}} \displaystyle=\  \displaystyle\frac{2\kappa(\tilde{\bm{X}}^{(s)})\|\tilde{\bm{X}}-\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})\|_{F}}{\|\bm{X}^{*}\|_{2}}\cdot\frac{1}{\frac{2}{\kappa(\bm{X}^{*})}-\frac{\|\bm{X}^{*}-\tilde{\bm{X}}\|_{2}}{\|\bm{X}^{*}\|_{2}}-\frac{\|\bm{X}^{*}-\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})\|_{2}}{\|\bm{X}^{*}\|_{2}}} \displaystyle\overset{(b)}{\leq}\  \displaystyle\frac{\tau_{1}(\tau_{2}-1)}{\tau_{1}(\tau_{2}+1)-\tau_{2}+1}\frac{\kappa(\tilde{\bm{X}}^{(s)})\|\tilde{\bm{X}}-\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})\|_{F}}{\|\bm{X}^{*}\|_{2}} $$

where (a) follows after normalizing both the numerator and the denominator with $\|\tilde{\bm{X}}^{(s)}\|_{2}$ . Moreover, (b) follows from (14), Lemma 4 and $p_{2}=\Omega(\tau^{4}_{2}n/\theta^{2})$ . Next, we provide a bound on $\kappa(\tilde{\bm{X}}^{(s)})$ , and we do so by first bounding $\kappa(\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}}))$ . By Lemma 4 and Lemma 3, we have

$$ \displaystyle\kappa(\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}}))=\frac{\|\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})\|_{2}}{\sigma_{n}(\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}}))}\leq\frac{\|\bm{X}^{*}\|_{2}+\|\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})-\bm{X}^{*}\|_{2}}{\sigma_{n}(\bm{X}^{*})-\|\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})-\bm{X}^{*}\|_{2}} \displaystyle=\frac{\|\bm{X}^{*}\|_{2}+\|\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})-\bm{X}^{*}\|_{2}}{\|\bm{X}^{*}\|_{2}/\kappa(\bm{X}^{*})-\|\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})-\bm{X}^{*}\|_{2}}\leq\frac{\tau_{1}+1}{\frac{\tau_{1}(\tau_{2}-1)}{\tau_{2}+1}-1} $$

Upon assuming $\tau_{1}\geq 10$ and $\tau_{2}\geq 10$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\kappa(\tilde{\bm{X}}^{(s)}) \displaystyle\!\leq\!\frac{\|\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})\|_{2}\!+\!\|\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})\!-\!\tilde{\bm{X}}^{(s)}\|_{2}}{\sigma_{n}(\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}}))\!-\!\|\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})\!-\!\tilde{\bm{X}}^{(s)}\|_{2}}\!\leq\!\frac{1+\|\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})-\tilde{\bm{X}}^{(s)}\|_{F}/\|\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})\|_{2}}{1/\kappa(\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}}))-\|\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})-\tilde{\bm{X}}^{(s)}\|_{F}/\|\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})\|_{2}} \displaystyle\overset{(a)}{\leq}\frac{1+9/32}{79/121-9/32}<4. $$

For (a), we used (13) and the fact that $\|\bm{D}^{(s)}-\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F}\leq 1/4$ . To conclude, we have

$$ \displaystyle\|\mathrm{Polar}(\bm{D}^{*}\tilde{\bm{X}}\tilde{\bm{X}}^{(s)\top})-\mathrm{Polar}(\bm{D}^{*}\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})\tilde{\bm{X}}^{(s)\top})\|_{F} \displaystyle<\frac{12\|\tilde{\bm{X}}-\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})\|_{F}}{\|\bm{X}^{*}\|_{2}}\leq\frac{12\|\bm{X}^{*}-\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})\|_{F}}{\|\bm{X}^{*}\|_{2}}. $$

Next, we turn our focus to $\|\mathrm{Polar}(\bm{D}^{*}\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})\tilde{\bm{X}}^{(s)\top})-\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F}$ , which is the second term of (15). We first introduce the following lemma, which is borrowed from Ravishankar et al., (2020):

#### Lemma 5 (Approximation error for dictionary (See the proof of Lemma 2.4 in Ravishankar et al., (2020))).

For any matrix $\bm{X}^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$ and $\bm{Y}=\bm{D}^{*}\bm{X}^{*}$ where $\bm{D}^{*}\in\mathbb{O}^{n}$ , consider an approximation $\bm{X}$ to $\bm{X}^{*}$ with $\bm{E}:=\left(\bm{X}-\bm{X}^{*}\right)/\|\bm{X}^{*}\|_{2}$ satisfying $\|\bm{E}\|_{F}<{1}/{\kappa^{2}\left(\bm{X}^{*}\right)}$ . Then, for some constant $C_{T}>0$ , $\bm{D}=\mathrm{Polar}(\bm{Y}\bm{X}^{\top})$ satisfies:

$$ \displaystyle\|\bm{D}-\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F}\leq \displaystyle\frac{\kappa(\bm{X}^{*})^{4}}{2}\frac{\left\|\bm{X}^{*}\bm{E}^{\top}-\bm{E}\bm{X}^{*\top}\right\|_{F}}{\|\bm{X}^{*}\|_{2}}+C_{T}\|\bm{E}\|^{2}_{F}. $$

To invoke Lemma 5, let $\tilde{\bm{E}}^{(s)}=\frac{\tilde{\bm{X}}^{(s)}-\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})}{\|\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})\|_{2}}$ , and notice that

$$ \displaystyle\|\tilde{\bm{E}}^{(s)}\|_{F} \displaystyle\overset{(a)}{\leq}\frac{9}{8}\|\bm{D}^{(s)}-\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F}\leq\frac{9}{32}\leq\left(\frac{79}{121}\right)^{2}\overset{(b)}{\leq}\frac{1}{\kappa^{2}(\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}}))}. $$

where (a) and (b) follow from (13) and (16), respectively. Therefore, Lemma 5 can be invoked:

$$ \displaystyle\|\mathrm{Polar}(\bm{D}^{*}\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})\tilde{\bm{X}}^{(s)\top})- \displaystyle\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F}\leq\frac{\kappa(\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}}))^{4}}{2}\frac{\left\|\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})\tilde{\bm{E}}^{(s)\top}-\tilde{\bm{E}}^{(s)}\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})^{\top}\right\|_{F}}{\|\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})\|_{2}}+C_{T}\|\bm{E}\|^{2}_{F}. $$

By recalling $\mathrm{supp}(\tilde{\bm{X}}^{(s)})=\mathrm{supp}(\bm{X}^{*})$ , we follow the same argument in the proof of Lemma 2 and conclude that

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\left\|\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})\tilde{\bm{E}}^{(s)\top}-\tilde{\bm{E}}^{(s)}\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})^{\top}\right\|_{F}}{2\|\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})\|_{2}}\leq\frac{\max_{1\leq k\leq n}\left\|\bm{M}_{k}\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})\tilde{\bm{M}}_{k}\right\|_{2}\|\tilde{\bm{E}}^{(s)}\|_{F}}{\|\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})\|_{2}}, $$

where $\bm{M}_{k}$ and $\tilde{\bm{M}}_{k}$ are defined in the same way as in the proof of Lemma 2. Since both $\bm{M}_{k}$ and $\tilde{\bm{M}}_{k}$ are linear operators, we have

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\max_{1\leq k\leq n}\left\|\bm{M}_{k}\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})\tilde{\bm{M}}_{k}\right\|_{2}}{\|\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})\|_{2}}\leq\frac{\max_{1\leq k\leq n}\left\|\bm{M}_{k}\bm{X}^{*}\tilde{\bm{M}}_{k}\right\|_{2}+\|\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})-\bm{X}^{*}\|_{2}}{\|\bm{X}^{*}\|_{2}(1-\|\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})-\bm{X}^{*}\|_{F}/\|\bm{X}^{*}\|_{2})} \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\ \frac{\tau_{1}}{\tau_{1}-1}\!\left(\frac{\max_{1\leq k\leq n}\left\|\bm{M}_{k}\bm{X}^{*}\tilde{\bm{M}}_{k}\right\|_{2}}{\|\bm{X}^{*}\|_{2}}\!+\!\frac{1}{\tau_{1}}\right) $$

Following the proof of Lemma 2, we have that with probability $1-2\exp(\log n-n)$ and $p_{2}=\Omega(\tau^{4}_{2}n/\theta^{2})$

$$ \frac{\max_{1\leq k\leq n}\left\|\bm{M}_{k}\bm{X}^{*}\tilde{\bm{M}}_{k}\right\|_{2}}{\|\bm{X}^{*}\|_{2}}\leq\frac{\tau_{2}+1}{\tau_{2}-1}\sqrt{\theta}. $$

Combined with (17), we have

$$ \displaystyle\|\mathrm{Polar}(\bm{D}^{*}\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})\tilde{\bm{X}}^{(s)\top})-\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F}\leq\frac{\kappa(\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}}))^{4}}{2}\frac{\left\|\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})\tilde{\bm{E}}^{(s)\top}-\tilde{\bm{E}}^{(s)}\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})^{\top}\right\|_{F}}{\|\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})\|_{2}}+C_{T}\|\tilde{\bm{E}}^{(s)}\|^{2}_{F} \displaystyle\leq\left(\frac{\tau_{1}}{\tau_{1}-1}\left(\frac{\tau_{2}+1}{\tau_{2}-1}\sqrt{\theta}+\frac{1}{\tau_{1}}\right)\kappa(\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}}))^{4}+C_{T}\|\tilde{\bm{E}}^{(s)}\|_{F}\right)\|\tilde{\bm{E}}^{(s)}\|_{F} $$

Therefore, we have a bound for the second term on the right-hand side of (15). Recall that $\kappa(\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}}))\leq\frac{\tau_{1}+1}{\frac{\tau_{1}(\tau_{2}-1)}{\tau_{2}+1}-1}$ due to (16) and $0<\theta<1/2$ . Therefore, similar to the proof of Lemma 2, for sufficiently large $\tau_{1}$ and $\tau_{2}$ and $\|\tilde{\bm{E}}^{(s)}\|_{F}\leq\frac{1}{10{C_{T}}}$ , (15) can be rewritten as

$$ \displaystyle\|\bm{D}^{(s+1)}-\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F} \displaystyle\overset{(a)}{\leq}0.9\|\bm{D}^{(s)}-\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F}\!+\!\frac{12\|\bm{X}^{*}-\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\bm{X}})\|_{F}}{\|\bm{X}^{*}\|_{2}} \displaystyle\leq 0.9\|\bm{D}^{(s)}-\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F}+12\|\bm{P}^{(s)}\bm{A}^{*}-\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F}, $$

where (a) follows from (13). This completes the proof of the induction step (8). For each induction step, our analysis holds with probability at least $1-O\left(\exp(\log p_{2}-n)\right)$ . After taking the union bound, the first $T$ steps of the induction hold with probability at least $1-O\left(\exp(\log T+\log p_{2}-n)\right)$ , which is $1-n^{-\omega(1)}$ when $T=O(n^{\beta})$ and $p_{2}=O(n^{\gamma})$ . Finally, we use (20) to complete the proof of Theorem 3. To this goal, notice that

$$ \displaystyle\|\bm{A}^{(s+1)}-\bm{A}^{*}\|_{F}=\left\|\bm{P}^{(s+1)-1}\bm{D}^{(s+1)}-\left(\mathcal{L}((\bm{A}^{*}\bm{A}^{*\top})^{-1})^{\top}\right)^{-1}\bm{D}^{*}\right\|_{F} \displaystyle\leq\|\bm{D}^{(s+1)}-\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F}+\left\|\bm{P}^{(s+1)-1}-\left(\mathcal{L}((\bm{A}^{*}\bm{A}^{*\top})^{-1})^{\top}\right)^{-1}\right\|_{F} \displaystyle\leq 0.9\|\bm{D}^{(s)}\!-\!\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F}\!+\!O\left(\|\bm{P}^{(s)}\bm{A}^{*}\!-\!\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F}\right)\!+\!O\left(\left\|\bm{P}^{(s+1)}-\mathcal{L}\left(\left(\bm{A}^{*}\bm{A}^{*\top}\right)^{-1}\right)^{\top}\right\|_{F}\right) $$

Via a similar argument, we can write

$$ \displaystyle\|\bm{D}^{(s)}-\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F}\leq\  \displaystyle\|\bm{A}^{(s)}-\bm{A}^{*}\|_{F}+O\left(\left\|\bm{P}^{(s)}-\mathcal{L}\left(\left(\bm{A}^{*}\bm{A}^{*\top}\right)^{-1}\right)^{\top}\right\|_{F}\right). $$

Combining (21) and (22), we have

$$ \displaystyle\|\bm{A}^{(s+1)}-\bm{A}^{*}\|_{F}\leq 0.9\|\bm{A}^{(s)}-\bm{A}^{*}\|_{F} \displaystyle+O\left(\left\|\bm{P}^{(s)}-\mathcal{L}\left(\left(\bm{A}^{*}\bm{A}^{*\top}\right)^{-1}\right)^{\top}\right\|_{F}\!+\!\|\bm{P}^{(s)}\bm{A}^{*}\!-\!\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F}\!+\!\left\|\bm{P}^{(s+1)}-\mathcal{L}\left(\left(\bm{A}^{*}\bm{A}^{*\top}\right)^{-1}\right)^{\top}\right\|_{F}\right) $$

By invoking Lemma 3, we can bound $\|\bm{P}^{(s)}\bm{A}^{*}-\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F}$ , $\left\|\bm{P}^{(s)}-\mathcal{L}\left(\left(\bm{A}^{*}\bm{A}^{*\top}\right)^{-1}\right)^{\top}\right\|_{F}$ , and $\left\|\bm{P}^{(s+1)}-\mathcal{L}\left(\left(\bm{A}^{*}\bm{A}^{*\top}\right)^{-1}\right)^{\top}\right\|_{F}$ with $O\left(\frac{\hat{\kappa}^{6}}{\theta}\sqrt{\frac{n}{p_{1}+T}}\right)$ . This completes the proof. $\hfill\square$

### 3.3 Proof of Theorem 2

Theorem 2 is a special case of Theorem 3, where we use one pre-calculated preconditioner throughout. In particular, it is easy to see that (20) in the proof of Theorem 3 holds after replacing $\bm{P}^{(s)}$ with $\bm{P}$ :

$$ \|\bm{D}^{(s+1)}-\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F}\leq 0.9\|\bm{D}^{(s)}-\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F}+12\|\bm{P}\bm{A}^{*}-\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F}, $$

Therefore, we have

$$ \displaystyle\|\bm{D}^{(s+1)}-\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F} \displaystyle\leq 0.9\|\bm{D}^{(s)}-\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F}+12\|\bm{P}\bm{A}^{*}-\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F} \displaystyle\leq 0.9^{s}\|\bm{D}^{(0)}\!-\!\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F}\!+\!\left(0.9\!+...+\!0.9^{s}\right)12\|\bm{P}\bm{A}^{*}-\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F} \displaystyle=0.9^{s}\|\bm{D}^{(0)}-\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F}+O(\|\bm{P}\bm{A}^{*}-\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F}). $$

Given the above inequality, one can use the same argument as in (21) and (22) to establish the linear convergence of $\bm{A}^{(s)}$ . The details are omitted for brevity. $\hfill\square$

## 4 Numerical Experiments

In this section, we validate our theoretical results using synthetic and real data. All experiments are performed on a MacBook Pro 2021 with the Apple M1 Pro chip and a 16GB unified memory for a serial implementation in MATLAB 2022a. The code is available at: https://github.com/lianggeyuleo/CompleteDL.git.

### 4.1 Synthetic Dataset

We validate our theoretical results using synthetic dataset. We consider the generative model $\bm{Y}=\bm{A}^{*}\bm{X}^{*}$ where $\bm{A}^{*}$ is a randomly generated orthogonal or full-rank dictionary. Moreover, $\bm{X}^{*}$ is generated from a Gaussian-Bernoulli distribution followed by a truncation step, where the entries $\bm{X}^{*}_{ij}$ with $|\bm{X}^{*}_{ij}|<\Gamma=0.3$ are replaced by $\bm{X}^{*}_{ij}=\mathrm{sgn}(\bm{X}^{*}_{ij})\Gamma$ . Consequently, the threshold $\zeta$ in each algorithm is set to $\Gamma/2=0.15$ .

First, we compare the efficiency of our method in solving ODL to other state-of-the-art techniques. In this experiment, we vary the signal dimension $n$ from 50 to 800 and set the sample size $p=100n$ , which corresponds to the linear-sample size condition in Theorem 1. We invoke the warm-start method in Algorithm 4 to generate the initial points. For each trial, we stop the algorithm when the consecutive iterates are close to each other ( $\|\bm{D}^{(t-1)}-\bm{D}^{(t-1)}\|_{2}\leq 10^{-7}$ ) and record the running time and final error ( $\|\bm{D}^{(T)}-\bm{D}^{*}\|_{F}$ ).

Many algorithms for dictionary learning exhibit poor scalability in this setting. For instance, the convergence time of KSVD method Aharon et al., (2006), which is perhaps the most well-known alternating minimization algorithm for dictionary learning, exceeds 300 seconds even for our smallest instance $n=50$ . Another example is the alternating minimization based on $\ell_{1}$ -regularization Agarwal et al., (2016), which suffers from a similar scalability issue. Instead, in Figure 3, we consider two other candidate algorithms that have comparable scalability with ours: Gradient-based method Arora et al., (2015): In this method, the dictionary update step (Step 4 in Algorithm 1) is replaced by a gradient step $\bm{D}^{(t+1)}=\bm{D}^{(t)}-\eta\nabla_{\bm{D}^{(t)}}L$ where $L$ is the objective of ODL. Here, we pick $\eta=10^{-5}$ after fine-tuning, which is the largest step-size to guarantee convergence in practice. $\ell_{4}$ -maximization-based method Zhai et al., (2020): The work Zhai et al., (2020) introduces a projected gradient ascend for maximizing the objective function $f(\bm{D})=\|\bm{D}^{\top}\bm{Y}\|^{4}_{4}$ . This method is shown to have superior performance compared to SPAMS Jenatton et al., (2010) and Subgradient method Bai et al., (2018). As can be seen in Figure 3, our method converges faster while achieving a smaller error. Particularly, the gradient-based method will require more time to converge, while $\ell_{4}$ maximization is restricted by its poor accuracy.

Finally, we numerically test the stability and sample complexity of our algorithm as $\bm{A}^{*}$ becomes increasingly ill-conditioned. In Figure 5 (right), we present the results, illustrating the sample size required to achieve a final error of $\frac{\left\lVert\bm{A}^{(T)}-\bm{A}^{*}\right\rVert_{F}}{\left\lVert\bm{A}^{*}\right\rVert_{F}}\leq 0.1$ as the condition number of $\bm{A}^{*}$ varies from 1 to 1000. Surprisingly, our practical findings indicate that the relationship between sample size and the condition number differs from what our theoretical framework suggests, showcasing a more favorable scenario in practice.

As illustrated in Figure 5 (left), our algorithm remains unaffected by the increasing condition number $\kappa(\bm{A}^{*})$ in the noiseless scenario. However, it encounters difficulties in recovering $\bm{A}^{*}$ when both noise and ill-conditioning are present. ### 4.2 Real Dataset

In this section, we showcase the performance of Algorithm 3 in learning a dictionary for the Landscape Dataset TheBlackMamba31, (2023) consisting of 7,000 colored images of different landscapes, 20 of which are set aside as test dataset. To gauge the quality of our learned dictionary, we use our dictionary to perform a denoising task on these images.

#### Dataset

Each figure in our dataset is a colored image of size $150\times 150\times 3$ . Instead of directly learning a dictionary for the whole dataset, we follow the procedure in Aharon et al., (2006) and divide each figure into 225 patches of size $10\times 10\times 3$ . Each patch is then reshaped into a $300\times 1$ vector. Collecting all 225 patches over all 7000 images results in 1,575,000 patch samples. We downsample this dataset to 10,000 patch samples so that KSVD can also be applied to this dataset. This results in a data matrix $\bm{Y}$ of size $300\times 10,000$ with $n=300$ and $p=10,000$ . Our goal is to learn a dictionary $\bm{A}$ of size $300\times 300$ for this data matrix.

#### Image Denoising

We gauge the quality of our learned dictionary by using it to denoise noisy images. Here, we corrupt each image with 50% missing pixels. In other words, we select 50% of the $150\times 150$ pixels in each image uniformly at random and then set the pixel values across all three RBG channels to $0$ . Our goal is to learn a dictionary and use it to denoise this image by filling in the missing pixels. For reconstruction, we choose a sparsity level of approximately 10%, which simply corresponds to 30 atoms for reconstruction. With a given dictionary, the reconstruction is done using a standard implementation of orthogonal matching pursuit (OMP) found in the SPAMS library in Matlab Mairal et al., (2007).

For both the image denoising examples in Figure 1 and Figure 7, we set $p_{1}=p_{2}=500$ in Algorithm 3 (corresponding to a batch size of 500), and run it for a total of $T=2000$ iterations, which took $125$ seconds for the constructed data matrix $\bm{Y}$ . We randomly sample 20 images from the dataset, which are then corrupted with noise. The images before and after the denoising are shown in the first two rows of Figure 7. Here we see that our learned dictionary reconstructs the original image almost exactly.

Additionally, we compare our learned dictionary with that of KSVD, which is implemented using a standard sparse learning library Mairal et al., (2007) in Matlab. We allow KSVD a total running time of $1100$ seconds. A comparison of denoised results using dictionaries learned with Algorithm 3 and KSVD are shown in Figure 1. Here, we also see that the dictionary learned by Algorithm 3 greatly outperforms KSVD, achieving a much better reconstruction of the original image despite being 10 times faster. Furthermore, we plot the similarity score between the reconstructed image and the original image versus the running time of both algorithms. In particular, at each iteration of both algorithms, we use the dictionary at that iteration to reconstruct a denoised image and compare it with the original. We see in Figure 6 that our algorithm achieves a similarity score of $0.9$ in 120 seconds, while KSVD can only achieve a similarity score of 0.28 in 2500 seconds.

*Figure 6: Similarity score between reconstructed image and original image We display the similarity score between the denoised image and the original one for our algorithm (left) and KSVD (right). As time progresses, the dictionary obtained from our algorithm improves, leading to increasingly better reconstructions. On the other hand, while the dictionary obtained from KSVD improves with time, the reconstruction quality exhibits a slower rate of improvement.*

#### Image Inpainting

To further gauge the efficacy of our learned dictionary, here we consider the more challenging task of inpainting. Here instead of corrupting each image with 50% of missing pixels, we opt to blackout entire pixel blocks. We segment each image into patches with dimensions of $25\times 25$ to facilitate inpainting for larger areas of obscured pixels. Much like our previous approach, we execute Algorithm 3 for a total of $T=2,000$ , which consumed approximately 2,100 seconds. For the reconstruction process, we maintain a sparsity level of approximately 10%, as we did previously.

Our reconstruction results are depicted in Figure 7. We randomly blackout blocks of dimensions $3\times 3$ , $5\times 5$ , and $10\times 10$ . In all three scenarios, the total count of obscured blocks equals the total number of patches. It is evident that for smaller blacked-out blocks, our dictionary performs well in reconstructing the images. However, when dealing with larger $10\times 10$ blocks, the inpainting task becomes more challenging. In this case, we observe that the reconstructed images exhibit some imperfections within the blacked-out regions.

## 5 Conclusion

In this paper, we study the dictionary learning problem, where the goal is to represent a given set of data samples as linear combinations of a few atoms from a learned dictionary. The existing algorithms for dictionary learning often lack scalability or provable guarantees. This paper shows that a simple alternating minimization algorithm provably solves both orthogonal and complete dictionary learning problems. Unlike other provably convergent algorithms for dictionary learning, our proposed method does not rely on any convex relaxation of the problem, and can be easily implemented in realistic scales. Through synthetic and realistic experiments on image denoising, we showcase the superiority of our proposed algorithm compared to the most commonly-used algorithms for dictionary learning.

## Appendix A Preliminary

To prove our main theorems, we will rely on several preliminary results from high-dimensional statistics and matrix perturbation theory, which will be essential for our arguments. We denote the sub-Gaussian norm and $L^{2}$ -norm of a random variable with $\|\cdot\|_{\psi_{2}}$ and $\|\cdot\|_{L^{2}}$ respectively.

#### Theorem 4 (Concentration of sample covariance matrix Vershynin, (2018)).

Let $\bm{x}$ be a sub-Gaussian random vector in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ with covariance matrix $\bm{\Sigma}$ , such that

$$ \|\langle\bm{x},\bm{z}\rangle\|_{\psi_{2}}\leq C_{ce}\|\langle\bm{x},\bm{z}\rangle\|_{L^{2}}\quad\text{for any }\bm{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, $$

for some $C_{ce}\geq 1$ . Let $\bm{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$ be a matrix whose columns have identical and independent distribution as $\bm{x}$ . Then, for any $u\geq 0$ and with probability at least $1-2\exp{(-u)}$ , we have

$$ \left\|\frac{1}{p}\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top}-\bm{\Sigma}\right\|_{2}\lesssim C_{ce}^{2}\left(\sqrt{\frac{n+u}{p}}+\frac{n+u}{p}\right)\|\bm{\Sigma}\|_{2} $$

.

#### Theorem 5 (Concentration of norm Vershynin, (2018)).

Let $\bm{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ be a random vector with independent, sub-Gaussian coordinates $\bm{x}_{i}$ that satisfy $\mathbb{E}\bm{x}_{i}^{2}=$ 1. Then, $\|\|\bm{x}\left\|{}_{2}-\sqrt{n}\right\|_{\psi_{2}}\leq CK^{2}$ , where $K=\max_{i}\left\|\bm{x}_{i}\right\|_{\psi_{2}}$ and $C$ is an absolute constant.

We next introduce a perturbation bound for the polar decomposition.

#### Theorem 6 (Perturbation bound for polar decomposition Li, (1995)).

Let $\bm{A},\tilde{\bm{A}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ be full rank matrices with polar decompositions $\bm{A}=\bm{U}\bm{P}$ and $\tilde{\bm{A}}=\tilde{\bm{U}}\tilde{\bm{P}}$ . Then

$$ \|\bm{U}-\tilde{\bm{U}}\|_{F}\leq\frac{2}{\sigma_{n}(\bm{A})+\sigma_{n}(\tilde{\bm{A}})}\|\bm{A}-\tilde{\bm{A}}\|_{F}. $$

Consider each column vector of $\bm{X}^{*}$ as a random vector. Upon defining $\Sigma_{\bm{X}^{*}}$ as the covariance matrix of $\bm{x}$ , we have $\Sigma_{\bm{X}}=\theta\sigma^{2}\bm{I}_{n}$ . $$ \displaystyle\left\|\langle\bm{X}^{*}_{(\cdot,i)},\bm{z}\rangle\right\|^{2}_{\psi_{2}} \displaystyle=\left\|\sum_{j=1}^{n}\bm{X}^{*}_{(j,i)}z_{j}\right\|^{2}_{\psi_{2}}\leq\sum_{j=1}^{n}z_{j}^{2}\left\|\bm{X}^{*}_{(j,i)}\right\|^{2}_{\psi_{2}}\leq C_{1}\sigma^{2}, $$

$$ \left\|\langle\bm{X}^{*}_{(\cdot,i)},\bm{z}\rangle\right\|^{2}_{L^{2}}=\mathbb{E}\langle\bm{X}^{*}_{(\cdot,i)},\bm{z}\rangle^{2}=\bm{z}^{\top}\Sigma_{\bm{X}^{*}}\bm{z}=\theta\sigma^{2}. $$

### B.4 Proof of Lemma 1

The $(i,j)$ -th entry $\left(\bm{D}^{\top}\bm{Y}\right)_{ij}$ of $\bm{D}^{\top}\bm{Y}$ can be written as

$$ \displaystyle\left(\bm{D}^{\top}\bm{Y}\right)_{ij}=\langle\bm{D}_{(\cdot,i)},\bm{Y}_{(\cdot,j)}\rangle=\underbrace{\langle\bm{D}_{(\cdot,i)},\bm{D}^{*}_{(\cdot,i)}\rangle\bm{X}^{*}_{ij}}_{:=\mathcal{A}_{ij}}+\underbrace{\sum_{k\neq i}\langle\bm{D}_{(\cdot,i)},\bm{D}^{*}_{(\cdot,k)}\rangle\bm{X}^{*}_{kj}}_{:=\mathcal{B}_{ij}}. $$

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{A}_{ij}=\langle\bm{D}_{(\cdot,i)},\bm{D}_{(\cdot,i)}\rangle\bm{X}^{*}_{ij}+\langle\bm{D}_{(\cdot,i)},\bm{D}^{*}_{(\cdot,i)}-\bm{D}_{(\cdot,i)}\rangle\bm{X}^{*}_{ij}=\bm{X}^{*}_{ij}+\langle\bm{D}_{(\cdot,i)},\bm{D}^{*}_{(\cdot,i)}-\bm{D}_{(\cdot,i)}\rangle\bm{X}^{*}_{ij}. $$

As a result, when $\bm{X}^{*}_{ij}=0$ , we have $\mathcal{A}_{ij}=0$ . Moreover, when $\bm{X}^{*}_{ij}\neq 0$ , we have $|\mathcal{A}_{ij}|\geq(1-\|\bm{D}^{*}-\bm{D}\|_{1,2})\Gamma\geq\frac{3\Gamma}{4}$ , where the last inequality holds for every $n\geq\frac{16}{\sigma^{2}\theta}$ . Note that this will lead to $\left|\left(\bm{D}^{\top}\bm{Y}\right)_{ij}\right|\geq|\mathcal{A}_{ij}|-|\mathcal{B}_{ij}|\geq\Gamma/2$ , thereby proving the statement. We have

$$ \displaystyle\left|\mathcal{B}_{ij}\right| \displaystyle=\left|\left\langle\bm{D}_{(\cdot,i)},\sum_{k\neq i}\bm{D}^{*}_{(\cdot,k)}\bm{X}^{*}_{kj}\right\rangle\right| \displaystyle=\left|\left\langle\bm{D}_{(\cdot,i)}-\bm{D}^{*}_{(\cdot,i)},\sum_{k\neq i}\bm{D}^{*}_{(\cdot,k)}\bm{X}^{*}_{kj}\right\rangle\right| \displaystyle\leq\left\|\bm{D}_{(\cdot,i)}-\bm{D}^{*}_{(\cdot,i)}\right\|_{2}\left\|\sum_{k\neq i}\bm{D}^{*}_{(\cdot,k)}\bm{X}^{*}_{kj}\right\|_{2} \displaystyle\leq\left\|\bm{D}_{(\cdot,i)}-\bm{D}^{*}_{(\cdot,i)}\right\|_{2}\left\|\sum_{k=1}^{n}\bm{D}^{*}_{(\cdot,k)}\bm{X}^{*}_{kj}\right\|_{2} \displaystyle=\left\|\bm{D}_{(\cdot,i)}-\bm{D}^{*}_{(\cdot,i)}\right\|_{2}\left\|\bm{Y}_{(\cdot,j)}\right\|_{2} \displaystyle=\left\|\bm{D}_{(\cdot,i)}-\bm{D}^{*}_{(\cdot,i)}\right\|_{2}\left\|\bm{X}_{(\cdot,j)}\right\|_{2}. $$

2: Set $\bm{v}=\frac{\bm{A}\bm{y}}{\sqrt{1+\bm{y}^{\top}\bm{A}\bm{y}}}$ , $\bm{A}^{\prime}=\bm{A}-\bm{v}\bm{v}^{\top}$ , $\bm{L}=\frac{\bm{L}}{\sqrt{(p_{1}+t)\theta\sigma^{2}}}$ , $\bm{w}=\bm{v}$ , and $b=1$ .

7: end for
